The salt spray had long since bleached Elias’s skin to the color of old parchment, but his eyes remained sharp, scanning the horizon for the faintest glimmer of hope or the darkest shadow of danger. For forty years, the lighthouse on Blackrock Point had been his cathedral, his prison, and his only companion. The rhythm of the tower was etched into his bones: the winding of the stairs, the polishing of the brass, the turning of the great Fresnel lens that cut through the night like a sword of light.

Tonight, the storm was unlike any he had seen in decades. The wind howled like a wounded beast, battering the stone walls with relentless fury. Rain lashed against the glass of the lantern room, distorting the beam into jagged streaks of white. Elias gripped the railing, his knuckles white, watching the waves crash against the base of the rock with terrifying power. He remembered the night his wife, Martha, had passed, her hand cold in his as the lighthouse beam swept over them one last time. He had promised to keep the light burning, not just for the ships, but for her memory.
